                                             I. ARGUMENT

TO THE HONORABLE LINDA H. BRITE AND LINDA J. BURGESS,
ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

        The Comanche Nation (“Nation”) seeks to protect its vast Tribal cultural resources on its

ancestral lands that will be directly crossed by this Project. The Nation urges the Public Utilities

Commission (“Commission” or “PUC”) to protect the Nation’s interests—and the interests of

Texas—by conditioning Joint Applicants’ amended Certificates of Convenience and Necessity

(“CCN”) on compliance with the vital cultural resource protection and preservation

recommendations made in its initial brief and restated below as Proposed Ordering Paragraphs.

Such measures are reasonable, enhance cultural and historic resource protections with no

material added costs to the Project, and promote the public interest of the State of Texas. 1

        While the Nation does not take a position on any particular route at issue in this

proceeding, the Nation implores the Commissioners to recognize what was admitted and proven

during the hearing in this proceeding—that the Nation is an affected community with respect to

the Project 2—and, accordingly, to issue an Order that reflects and protects the Nation’s interests,

the public interest, and the interest of the State of Texas.

        Joint Applicants claim that the Commission’s standard Ordering paragraphs are adequate

with respect to cultural and historic resources jeopardized by construction of the Project because

their environmental consultant employed the same standard methodology to identify cultural

does not justify perpetuating such inadequate or faulty practices. Joint Applicants specifically

cite to the “consistent” dataset 4 as adequate for comparison. However, consistent does not equate

to comprehensive. As Joint Applicants’ witness Russell Marusak admitted, absence from an

archeological database does not prove absence of archeological resources. 5 This “standard”

methodology of an applicant merely reviewing Texas Historical Commission records is

insufficient in light of the extensive historical presence of the Comanche in the Project area.

Furthermore, as he testified during the hearing, PUC Staff’s witness John Poole is not aware of

any proposed route that parallels cultural features—even though, as Mr. Poole agreed, cultural

resources and human remains are less likely to be disturbed when a transmission line is built

parallel to cultural features. 6 Given those circumstances, and the fact that Joint Applicants’

limited pre-application cultural resource identification process failed to yield significant

historical or cultural resources data (and was deficient, as described below), the pre-construction

survey work and the construction process itself must include Comanche Tribal monitors.

        The Environmental Assessment (“EA”) declares, and Joint Applicants’ witness Russell

Marusak acknowledged, that there is high potential for encountering cultural resources that have

not yet been identified within the Project area. 7 “There have been no boots on the ground surveys

for any portion of the study area,” 8 and Joint Applicants “cannot and have not” ruled out the

possibility that culturally significant Comanche resources exist in the Project area 9. Similarly,

 Mr. Poole agreed that additional groundwork on any route may yield additional cultural

resources. 10 Mr. Poole agreed during the hearing that cultural resources encountered along any

proposed route would be best known to Comanche Nation Tribal members. 11 Mr. Marusak

acknowledged that the Comanche Nation has historical and cultural ties to the Project area, and

agreed that Tribal consultation can assist in identifying cultural resources that might be otherwise

overlooked. 12 Mr. Marusak also agreed that tribes (like the Nation) may possess knowledge

regarding cultural resources that have not been included in public databases or publicly recorded

inventories. 13 Simply put, Comanches are uniquely qualified to identify and evaluate Comanche

cultural resources and their significance. Comanche Nation witness Steve Houser’s testimony

reinforces the unique and necessary perspective brought by Tribal monitors. Mr. Houser

emphasizes the importance of Tribal monitors in the identification of marker trees as a cultural

resource based upon their unique historical knowledge, training, and experience. 14 Their

expertise during the pre-construction and construction phases of the Project is vital to protecting

Comanche cultural resources and human remains.

         The extremely limited scope of Joint Applicants’ EA compels a more thorough

methodology for the pre-construction cultural resources survey to protect the interests of the

Nation, the public, and the State of Texas. The design of such a survey must include Comanche

Nation-approved Tribal monitors to better ensure that known and unknown Comanche cultural

resources can be identified and protected. 15 Furthermore, Comanche Nation-approved Tribal

         As Joint Applicants’ testimony and briefing make clear, they can readily absorb the costs

associated with Tribal monitors within the existing Project budget, including contingencies. In

Table 1 on page 43 of their Initial Brief, Joint Applicants compare the costs (and other factors) of

the nine routes they identified as “routes of interest” based on the hearing. These costs range

from $1.665B to $1.755B, or a range of $90M, 16 demonstrating that Joint Applicants do not view

$90M as a significant price difference. This analysis alone demonstrates that the Tribal

monitoring cost would be immaterial and absorbable. As Mr. Poole described it, the range of

costs in this case “would be the cost of the entire transmission line in other cases. We’re talking

like a hundred million dollars. That’s a pretty significant cost, but not as a percentage of the

overall project.” 17 Furthermore, Joint Applicants “applied a contingency of 10 percent and 15

percent in the cost model.” 18 The purpose of this cost contingency is to cover “‘an unanticipated

event or condition that may be encountered during the design and construction of the proposed

project’” 19–such as CCN conditions requiring Tribal monitors.

directly threatened) interests of the Comanche Nation, the public, and the State of Texas.

            For the foregoing reasons and those set forth in the Nation’s Initial Brief, the Nation

implores the Commissioners to comply with Texas public policy by adopting the following

proposed findings, conclusions, and Ordering paragraphs in its Order.

                                   II.    PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT

       1. PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission consider community values and historical

            values in determining whether to grant a CCN.

       2. The concept of “community values” includes values significant to affected communities.

       3. The Comanche Nation (“Nation”) is an affected community for purposes of this

            proceeding.

       4. In their efforts to provide notice to the public, Joint Applicants provided direct notice of

            the Project to 28 municipal governments and 15 county governments.

       5. As they acknowledge, Joint Applicants provided no notice to Tribal government officials

            of the Comanche Nation, an affected community.

       6. Joint Applicants did not notify, consult, or contact the Comanche Nation regarding the

            Project prior to the Nation’s intervention in this proceeding. Although Joint Applicants

            may have complied with the Texas Utilities Code and Administrative Code provisions

            specifically related to notice, by failing to notify an “affected community,” they failed to


20
     Id. at 249:17-21.
21

PUC Docket No. 59475

        solicit key information from the Tribe that would have better informed the Application

       and they failed to comply with the spirit of the law with respect to notice.

   7. The proposed Project stretches across a significant portion of Comanchería, the ancestral

       homelands of the Comanche that include a vast swath of present-day Texas.

   8. The Project area is rich with cultural and historical resources, many of which hold great

       cultural, historic, and spiritual significance to the Comanche Nation.

   9. Texas Historical Commission (“THC”) records are not comprehensive and do not include

       all existing cultural and historical resources in the Project area.

   10. Despite conducting a review of THC records, Joint Applicants failed to properly identify

       at least three existing cultural resource trinomials within 500 feet of the proposed

       centerline of the transmission line, demonstrating that even the THC record review—the

       only cultural resources study done to date—was insufficient.

   11. Although the Nation did not have an opportunity to bring its concerns about the Project to

       the attention of Joint Applicants or influence the Environmental Assessment, interested

       individuals who responded to the public interest questionnaire identified numerous

       landowner and local government concerns related to archeological and historic sites and

       the presence of cultural resources along several portions of the proposed routes, putting

       Joint Applicants on notice that cultural resource protection is a community value that

       mandates consideration in this proceeding.

   12. Construction of the Project poses a significant risk of destruction or desecration of

       Comanche cultural resources.

   13. Any damage to Comanche cultural resources during construction of the Project would

       harm the interests of both the Comanche Nation and the State of Texas.

Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 9
    14. Comanche cultural resources include “marker trees,” which are trees of ongoing spiritual

       and historical significance that were purposely shaped by Comanches to point towards

       important streams, sacred sites, and burial grounds.

   15. Comanche cultural resources also include red berry cedar trees (Juniperus pinchotii) and

       Texas mountain laurel trees (Dermatophyllum secundiflorum), which are used by

       Comanche Tribal members for ceremonial purposes.

   16. Tribal monitors are trained Native American representatives who observe construction,

       infrastructure, or environmental projects to protect cultural resources, ancestral sites, and

       human remains. They ensure compliance with cultural resource protection laws and

       inadvertent discovery plans, bridging traditional knowledge with modern archeology to

       prevent damage during construction. They are also used during projects to ensure that

       Indigenous knowledge and expertise are incorporated in cultural resources surveys,

       increasing the value and accuracy of a survey.

   17. The incorporation of Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors during the pre-

       construction cultural resources survey will enhance the survey and will likely result in

       more comprehensive, accurate, and thorough survey results.

   18. By improving the survey results, the incorporation of Tribal monitors during the pre-

       construction cultural resources survey will minimize the number of inadvertent

       discoveries during Project construction and reduce costs and delays that result from such

       inadvertent discoveries.

   19. The services of Tribal monitors during construction of the Project will protect cultural

       resources encountered during construction that have not been identified during the pre-

       construction survey.

Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 10
                            III. PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

   1. State law requires that the State of Texas “locate, protect, and preserve all sites, objects, .

       . . and locations of historical [and] archeological . . . interest, including but not limited to

       prehistoric and historical American Indian or aboriginal campsites, dwellings, and

       habitation sites [and] archeological sites of every character . . . .” Tex. Nat. Res. Code §

       191.002.

   2. It is the public policy and in the public interest of the State of Texas that reasonable

       conditions be imposed on the amended CCNs granted herein to locate, protect, and

       preserve Comanche cultural resources contained within the Project area.

   3. The Project must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the

       Comanche Nation as an “affected community” pursuant to 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

   4. The use of Tribal monitors during the cultural resources survey and during construction

       of the Project will best ensure Joint Applicants’ compliance with State law regarding the

       location, protection, and preservation of cultural and historical resources contained within

       the Project area.

                       IV. PROPOSED ORDERING PARAGRAPHS

       Consistent with the above Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, the Commission

issues the following orders.

   1. Joint Applicants must conduct a pre-construction cultural resources survey of the

       approved route prior to engaging in ground-disturbing activities.

   2. Joint Applicants must retain the services of Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors

       to assist and participate in the pre-construction cultural resources survey at Joint

       Applicants’ expense.

Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 11
    3. Participants in the pre-construction cultural resources survey for the Project shall be

       trained by the Texas Historic Tree Coalition regarding the identification of marker trees

       and shall include and document any marker trees identified during the cultural resources

       survey in the survey results.

   4. Joint Applicants must retain the services of Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors

       to conduct Tribal monitoring during all ground-disturbing activities during construction

       of the Project at Joint Applicants’ expense. Joint Applicants or their agents shall

       coordinate with such Tribal monitors and the Comanche Nation Tribal Historic

       Preservation Officer (“Comanche THPO”) and keep them adequately apprised regarding

       times, locations, and other details of construction necessary to perform their Tribal

       monitoring duties.

   5. Joint Applicants and their agents are prohibited from cutting, clearing, or otherwise

       damaging marker trees, red berry cedar trees (Juniperus pinchotii), or Texas mountain

       laurel trees (Dermatophyllum secundiflorum) unless they may fall into or touch the

       transmission line.

   6. Joint Applicants must minimize right-of-way clearing and minimize the amount of flora

       and fauna disturbed during construction.

   7. Joint Applicants must avoid affecting non-targeted vegetation or animal life when using

       chemical herbicides to control vegetation within the right-of-way and comply with the

       rules and guidelines established in the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide and Rodenticide Act

       and with the regulations of the Texas Department of Agriculture regarding herbicide use.




Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 12
    8. Joint Applicants must develop an Inadvertent Discovery Plan for construction of the

       Project in conjunction with the Comanche THPO and the THC that shall include, at a

       minimum, the following provisions:

           a. Immediate Stop-Work Protocol. Upon encountering a cultural resource or burial,
              construction shall not resume until after the resource or human remains have been
              adequately protected or avoided and, if the cultural resource or human remains are
              Native American, until after the affiliated Indian tribe agrees with the treatment
              plan for the cultural resource or human remains.
           b. Immediate Notification. Upon encountering a cultural resource or human remains,
              Joint Applicants or their representative shall immediately notify both the
              Comanche Nation Tribal Chairman and the Comanche THPO.
           c. Investigation. The Comanche THPO or their designee shall be granted physical
              access to investigate an inadvertent discovery of a cultural resource or human
              remains in situ.
           d. NAGPRA-Compliant Human Remains Provisions. Joint Applicants and their
              agents shall comply with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation
              Act, 25 U.S.C. Chapter 32.
           e. Tribal Monitors. Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors and the Comanche
              THPO shall be permitted to be on-site at the site of any inadvertent discovery.
           f. Cultural Affiliation Determination. The cultural affiliation of any inadvertent
              discovery shall be determined based on available information, including
              information provided by the Comanche Nation or other Indian tribes.
           g. Treatment and Disposition of Discovered Cultural Resources. Joint Applicants,
              the Comanche THPO, and the THC shall collaborate to develop specific
              provisions for the appropriate treatment and disposition of discovered cultural
              resources.
           h. Project Adjustment and Avoidance. In the event of an inadvertent discovery of a
              cultural resource or human remains, the Project route shall be adjusted within the
              right-of-way to avoid damage or destruction of the resource or remains to the
              maximum extent possible.
           i. Pre-Construction Training Requirements. Prior to commencing construction, Joint
              Applicants shall provide responsible parties and construction personnel with
              training regarding the cultural history of the Project area, the recognition of
              cultural resources, and the requirements of the Inadvertent Discovery Plan,
              including the steps to be followed in the event of an inadvertent discovery.
           j. Confidentiality Provisions. Any cultural resource-related information provided to
              Joint Applicants by the Comanche Nation or an agent thereof shall be treated as

Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 13
                confidential and shall not be disclosed by Joint Applicants except as required by
               law.
           k. Dispute Resolution. The Inadvertent Discovery Plan shall include fair and
              equitable dispute resolution procedures to be followed in the event of a dispute
              between Joint Applicants and an interested party regarding implementation of the
              Inadvertent Discovery Plan.
           l. Post-Discovery Reporting. Joint Applicants, the Comanche THPO, and the THC
              shall collaborate to develop post-discovery reporting procedures.
           m. Marker Trees. Marker trees are deemed a cultural resource for purposes of the
              Inadvertent Discovery Plan.
   9. Joint Applicants must provide the Comanche THPO with bi-weekly updates regarding the

       status of construction, impacted travel routes, and the anticipated date of Project

       completion.

   10. Joint Applicants must notify the Comanche Tribal Chairman and the Comanche THPO

       prior to any maintenance or other work after completion of the Project that will result in

       disturbance of ground not previously disturbed during construction, and must retain

       Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors to monitor such locations during the ground-

       disturbing activity.

                                  V. PRAYER FOR RELIEF

       The Comanche Nation respectfully prays that the Commission adopt the findings of fact,

conclusions of law, and Ordering paragraphs proposed by the Nation herein, and that the

Commission grant such further relief as the Nation may be justly entitled.

          of the Comanche Nation, an affected community.

     6. Joint Applicants did not notify, consult, or contact the Comanche Nation regarding the

         Project prior to the Nation's intervention in this proceeding. Although Joint Applicants

         may have complied with the Texas Utilities Code and Administrative Code provisions

     14. Comanche cultural resources include "marker trees," which are trees of ongoing spiritual

       and historical significance that were purposely shaped by Comanches to point towards

       important streams, sacred sites, and burial grounds.

    15. Comanche cultural resources also include red berry cedar trees (Juniperus pinchotii) and

       Texas mountain laurel trees (Dermatophyllum secundiflorum), which are used by

       Comanche Tribal members for ceremonial purposes.

    16. Tribal monitors are trained Native American representatives who observe construction,

       infrastructure, or environmental proj ects to protect cultural resources, ancestral sites, and

       human remains. They ensure compliance with cultural resource protection laws and

       inadvertent discovery plans, bridging traditional knowledge with modern archeology to

       prevent damage during construction. They are also used during projects to ensure that

       Indigenous knowledge and expertise are incorporated in cultural resources surveys,

       increasing the value and accuracy of a survey.

    17. The incorporation of Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors during the pre-

       construction cultural resources survey will enhance the survey and will likely result in

       more comprehensive, accurate, and thorough survey results.

    18. By improving the survey results, the incorporation of Tribal monitors during the pre-

       construction cultural resources survey will minimize the number of inadvertent

       discoveries during Project construction and reduce costs and delays that result from such

       inadvertent discoveries.

    19. The services of Tribal monitors during construction of the Project will protect cultural

       resources encountered during construction that have not been identified during the pre-

       construction survey.

                             III. PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

    1. State law requires that the State of Texas "locate, protect, and preserve all sites, obj ects, .

          and locations ofhistorical [andl archeological... interest, including but not limited to

       prehistoric and historical American Indian or aboriginal campsites, dwellings, and

       habitation sites [andl archeological sites of every character...." Tex. Nat. Res. Code §

        191.002.

   2. It is the public policy and in the public interest of the State of Texas that reasonable

       conditions be imposed on the amended CCNs granted herein to locate, protect, and

       preserve Comanche cultural resources contained within the Proj ect area.

   3. The Proj ect must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the

       Comanche Nation as an "affected community" pursuant to 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

   4. The use of Tribal monitors during the cultural resources survey and during construction

       of the Project will best ensure Joint Applicants' compliance with State law regarding the

       location, protection, and preservation of cultural and historical resources contained within

       the Proj ect area.

                        IV.    PROPOSED ORDERING PARAGRAPHS

       Consistent with the above Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, the Commission

issues the following orders.

    1. Joint Applicants must conduct a pre-construction cultural resources survey of the

       approved route prior to engaging in ground-disturbing activities.

   2. Joint Applicants must retain the services of Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors

       to assist and participate in the pre-construction cultural resources survey at Joint

       Applicants' expense.
